name: Mars Sample Return (NASA and ESA)
short_status: Cancelled: Congress declined to fund it in the appropriations bill signed on 23 January 2026, and ESA member states asked for the cancellation of the Earth Return Orbiter in March 2026. No replacement has been started.
tagline: NASA / ESA · Multinational · Programme · 2026 · Announced Cancelled
stats: probable lifecycle cost range found by the 2023 review board
given instead in the fiscal 2026 bill for Mars technology rather than MSR
sample tubes retrieved from the Martian surface

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: A multi-mission campaign by NASA and ESA to return sealed samples collected by the Perseverance rover. NASA's own page now uses the past tense: "Mars Sample Return was a plan for an ambitious, multi-mission campaign that would bring carefully selected Martian samples to Earth for the first time." That page was last updated on 3 August 2026.

facts.label: The samples
facts.value: Perseverance has taken samples in pairs where possible. One of each pair was placed at a backup depot on flat ground in Jezero Crater nicknamed Three Forks. NASA confirmed the tenth and final tube on 29 January 2023, less than six weeks after depot construction began; the last tube was imaged on the surface on 28 January 2023, sol 690. The depot also received an atmospheric sample and a witness tube. The other half of each pair stayed aboard the rover, which under the cancelled plan would have been the primary means of delivering samples to the Sample Retrieval Lander.

facts.label: The architecture as of 2025
facts.value: A Sample Retrieval Lander carrying a smaller Mars Ascent Vehicle powered by a radioisotope power system rather than solar panels, an orbiting sample container holding 30 tubes, and ESA's Earth Return Orbiter carrying a NASA-built Capture, Containment and Return System to catch the container in Mars orbit and seal it inside an Earth Entry System.

facts.label: The second review board
facts.value: MSR Independent Review Board 2, chaired by Orlando Figueroa, reported in September 2023. Its programmatic assessment put $8 billion to $11 billion as the probable total lifecycle cost at 50 to 80 per cent confidence, and found a "near zero probability" of the Earth Return Orbiter or the Sample Retrieval Lander meeting their 2027 and 2028 launch readiness dates, with 2030 dates possible given adequate funding.

facts.label: Where 2040 came from
facts.value: Not from the review board. In NASA's response of 15 April 2024, the agency said that "given the Fiscal Year 2025 budget and anticipated budget constraints, as well as the need to maintain a balanced science portfolio, the current mission design will return samples in 2040." Administrator Bill Nelson's line in the same release was: "The bottom line is, an $11 billion budget is too expensive, and a 2040 return date is too far away."

facts.label: The alternatives study
facts.value: NASA solicited alternative architectures from industry and its own centres in 2024 and accepted 11 studies in September 2024. A strategic review team led by Maria Zuber assessed them.

facts.label: The January 2025 decision
facts.value: On 7 January 2025 NASA announced it would carry two landing architectures forward in parallel: one reusing the sky crane system flown by Curiosity and Perseverance, the other buying a commercial lander. NASA said it expected to confirm the programme and its design in the second half of 2026. That confirmation never happened.

facts.label: The budget request that killed it
facts.value: The Trump administration's fiscal year 2026 budget request, released in May 2025, proposed cancelling MSR outright as part of a proposed 47 per cent cut to NASA science, from $7.334 billion to just over $3.9 billion.

facts.label: What Congress actually did
facts.value: The final fiscal 2026 bill rejected most of the proposed NASA cuts, giving the agency $24.438 billion and science $7.25 billion, but endorsed the cancellation of MSR. The accompanying report directed NASA to spend $110 million from a Mars Future Missions account "to support radar, spectroscopy, entry, descent, and landing systems, and translational precursor technologies". A House version had proposed $300 million.

facts.label: Enactment
facts.value: The Senate passed H.R. 6938, a three-bill minibus containing the Commerce, Justice and Science bill, by 82 votes to 15 on 15 January 2026, after the House passed it 397 to 28 on 8 January. The President signed it on 23 January 2026.

facts.label: NASA's reaction
facts.value: Administrator Jared Isaacman said in an interview reported on 16 February 2026 that "with near clarity now on the human exploration focus on the moon, we can free up some of our resources to consider how we would go and retrieve the Mars samples", adding "step one is closing out the old program". Asked about MSR at a 13 February 2026 news conference he said, "Am I interested in getting those samples back? You bet."

facts.label: ESA's side
facts.value: ESA had contracted Airbus Defence and Space in October 2020 for 491 million euros to build the Earth Return Orbiter. After the US funding decision, ESA's Director of Human and Robotic Exploration Daniel Neuenschwander said Mars Sample Return "is currently not planned to be continued". Following the 345th ESA Council meeting, reported on 28 March 2026, he said member states had "asked for the cancellation of the Earth Return Orbiter mission", with talks under way with Airbus about reusing technology such as the electric propulsion system.

facts.label: The authorisation bill
facts.value: On 4 March 2026 the Senate Commerce Committee advanced an amended S. 933 that directs the formal termination of the old MSR programme and calls for a new one, capped at $8 billion in total, required to use "existing flight-proven technologies" and limiting international contributions that would "unduly increase" cost and risk, with a plan due 120 days after enactment. As of 23 August 2026 we found no evidence the bill has been enacted or that NASA has begun such a programme.

facts.label: Fiscal 2027
facts.value: NASA's fiscal year 2027 request, released 3 April 2026, again asks for $110 million for Mars Future Missions but proposes to spend it on lower-cost science missions rather than MSR technologies, including a solicitation planned for October 2026 for a Mars mission launching in 2030 under a $220 million cost cap. Four senators wrote asking appropriators for at least $400 million, warning of "severe and irreversible harm" to US Mars capability.

facts.label: Industry position
facts.value: Lockheed Martin says it proposed returning the samples for under $3 billion. Whitley Poyser, the company's director of exploration, said on 13 April 2026 that the plan leveraged "proven, demonstrated technologies" and that "we still very much stand behind it". NASA has made no award.

facts.label: Dates and time zone
facts.value: Dates here are US Eastern-time publication and legislative dates, which for these events do not differ from UTC by more than one calendar day. Congressional votes and signings are recorded in Washington local time.

timeline: Perseverance builds the first sample depot on another world at Three Forks in Jezero Crater, laying ten sealed tubes on the ground as a backup set. NASA confirms the tenth and final tube on 29 January 2023, less than six weeks after the work began.

The second Mars Sample Return Independent Review Board reports: $8 billion to $11 billion probable lifecycle cost, near-zero probability of the 2027 and 2028 launch readiness dates, no credible cost, schedule or technical baseline within likely funding.

NASA publishes its response. Nelson calls $11 billion too expensive and a 2040 return too far away, and asks industry and JPL for cheaper architectures. NASA states that under its budget outlook the existing design would return samples in 2040.
NASA accepts 11 alternative architecture studies from industry and its own centres. A strategic review team led by Maria Zuber assesses them.

NASA announces it will carry two landing options forward in parallel, sky crane and commercial lander, with a smaller ascent vehicle, a 30-tube orbiting sample container and a radioisotope power source, and says it expects to confirm the programme in the second half of 2026.
The administration's fiscal year 2026 budget request proposes cancelling MSR and cutting NASA science by 47 per cent.

At the American Geophysical Union meeting, Perseverance officials say the rover is in excellent shape and continuing to collect samples despite having no plan for their return. Six empty tubes remain available and two filled tubes are still unsealed. Deputy project manager Steve Lee says the rover is being certified to drive at least 100 km, a distance derived from the abandoned MSR rendezvous studies.

The Senate passes the fiscal 2026 minibus containing the Commerce, Justice and Science bill by 82 votes to 15. The bill restores most NASA science funding but endorses the cancellation of MSR, substituting $110 million for Mars Future Missions.

The President signs the minibus. MSR is now unfunded law. The congressional Planetary Science Caucus co-chairs say they are "disappointed" that the highest-priority mission of the planetary decadal survey has been dropped.

The Senate Commerce Committee advances a NASA authorisation bill directing formal termination of the old MSR programme and creation of a new one with an $8 billion cap and a requirement to use flight-proven technology.
European Spaceflight reports that ESA member states have asked for the cancellation of the Earth Return Orbiter, and that ESA has opened talks with Airbus about reusing technology from it.

NASA's fiscal 2027 request keeps Mars Future Missions at $110 million but redirects it to small capped science missions rather than sample-return technology. Four senators write asking appropriators for at least $400 million, warning of "severe and irreversible harm" to the United States' ability to land on Mars.
